items.title: Tour de Pologne: Jonathan Milan wins fast and furious sprint on stage 2
items.content:
A long, utterly devastating surge of power saw Jonathan Milan (Lidl-Trek) easily fend off the opposition and come through a dangerous late corner perfectly placed for a second straight bunch sprint victory in the Tour de Pologne.

Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) tried hard to anticipate the race leader's last blast for the finish, but after chasing down XDS-Astana's Matteo Malucelli, the Frenchman once again proved powerless to stop the Italian national champion, who was already well ahead.

Given his superiority in the sprint, once a day-long four-rider breakaway had been reeled in, Milan's biggest obstacle was likely getting through a full U-turn corner at 400 metres to go unscathed, upright and well-positioned for the final kick - which he successfully did.

Once Milan opened up his sprint from third place behind Ivan García Cortina (Movistar), Magnier was seemingly in no position to answer, with the Italian doubling up on his stage 1 victory on the second-placed Frenchman, once again by several bike lengths.

"Once again I have to say thanks to my teammates, we managed really well," Milan said later in an audio file provided by his team.

"I was a bit nervous and worried about getting boxed in in the last three kilometres when there were big roads. It was easy to get lost in this kind of washing machine effect. But we always stayed together, the team always pulled for me."

"Those last 450 metres - I was surprised by the gap I got on the guys from Astana. But I had a good start to my sprint and even if it was a super-long one, it went really well."

On a very flat stage with no classified climbs and 91 metres above sea level being the high point of the entire day, the sprinters were always going to be itching for a second straight chance at victory. But neither a spell of brief midday rainfall nor that knowledge of the likely outcome deterred four breakaway riders from making a bid for freedom all the same.

Jonas Rutsch (Lotto-Intermarché), Anton Schiffer (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Polish National Team duo Radoslaw Frątczak and Patryk Stosz were the four who opted to go from distance almost from the gun. However, in a rerun of stage 1's early move, as soon as the break reached around 90 seconds' advantage, Lidl-Trek began tapping out a steady pace behind, evidently to ensure the sprinters in general and Milan in particular wouldn't miss out on such a great opportunity.

Up in the break, the two Poles were the keenest to claim the intermediate sprints that followed, seemingly taking turns to cross the line in first place. Meanwhile the peloton trundled along behind on a series of dense woodland and country roads, waiting for the right moment to light up the pace.

That process began around 65 kilometres to go, as Lidl-Trek and Soudal-QuickStep increased speed steadily and quickly reduced the four riders' gap from 90 to 40 seconds. That didn't stop KoM leader Dries De Bondt (Jayco-AlUla), though, from deciding it was time to bridge across and breathe some more life into the four-rider move.

Not helped by the relentlessly flat terrain along broad A-roads, the Belgian finally made it across after a 15-kilometre pursuit, just as Stosz fell out of the running in the break due to a mechanical. Stosz's teammate Frątczak was still in the thick of it, though, picking up the final intermediate sprint at Goleniów in another short, sharp skirmish.

De Bondt certainly played a critical role in keeping the break alive, taking very long turns on the front on an interminable series of flat highways, as EF, third on Monday with Noah Hobbs behind Milan and Magnier, also showed an interest in chasing behind. Eventually, the combined effort by the sprinters' teams had its near-inevitable effect and finally squeezed all the life out of the break at just under 15 kilometres to go, when observed by vast crowds of holidaymakers, the last of the four ahead were caught.

The series of well-surfaced highways leading to the North Sea coast was ideal for the sprinters' teams to keep things under control in the finale, particularly as NSN and Tudor helped ensure there were no late challengers. The sunshine beat down as the peloton tore across one vast bridge into Szczecin at speeds touching 60 km/h, even if the constantly switching of road-width from four to two lanes and back up again provided perfect conditions for a full-scale washing-machine effect in the bunch.

Netcompany-Ineos made a determined bid for Sam Welsford on the right of the road with three kilometres to go, trying to anticipate the more technical finale. Yet their effort crumpled as Decathlon CGA CMN began bossing the front and the pack swung over another long road bridge and onto a fast but brief section of downhill.

Powering through for Astana on the left-hand side in the final kilometre, Malucelli was perfectly positioned to make it first into the critical U-turn and out the other side. But Milan, too, had made it through the U-turn well-placed and ready to strike, and after a second devastating victory that came just seconds later for the Lidl-Trek star, the odds of Milan taking a third on stage 3's ultra-flat stage are almost equally high.

Hello and welcome to the Cyclingnews live coverage of the Tour de France Femmes time trial.

As always, we will have full live coverage of all the action from the 21km individual time trial to Dijon.

We are expecting some great individual performances but also a GC battle as every second counts.

Read our special TT preview for details of the 21km course and the riders in action.

Riders face extra pre-race checks by race judges after suspicions that some riders are looking for an extra marginal gains.

This is the map of the 21km time trial from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon through the Côte d’Or vineyards on central France.

Romina Hinojosa (Lotto Intermarché Ladies) is the first of the 139 riders to start the TT.

She rolls down the start ramp at 14:51CEST local time.

The Cyclingnews live coverage includes a Race Situation box with all the start times, the intermediate times and the finish time.

Our live updates will give you all the inside information on the TT, with details and analysis of the performances and what the time gians and time losses mean for the GC battle.

Early today, the riders were allowed to train and recon the course for a final time, to have a final look at the key corners and sectors.

This is the technical start to the TT. Precious seconds can be lost here.

Matilda Price and Dani Ostanek are on the ground in France, gathering all the best TDFF news, reaction and producing some great analysis.

Matilda wrote this special feature on the Tour starting in Switzerland and what that means for the race and for Swiss cycling. It's a fascinating read as we wait for the TT to begin.

We're loving the bidon hunting vibes at the TDFF.

It's 10 minutes to the start of the time trial and many riders are already warming up near their buses.

The fans and ice vests are out in the shade of the team buses because it is 34C on the ground in central France.

That heat adds an extra difficulty to the stage alongside the need to push at 100%, bike handling and those huge aero helmets.

Time trials are a test of many skills and that's why they're so fascinating.

tick, tock, tick, tock. It's almost time for the TT to begin.

There are 138 riders left in the race and they will start at 1-minutew intervals, with the last 20 riders starting at 2-minute intervals.

These are some key rider start times.

Romina Hinojosa (Lotto Intermarché Ladies) starts her ride. She is the first rider off.

Who is your pick for the race against the clock?

Have your say and take part in our poll at the top of our live coverage.

I voted for Zoe Bäckstedt because I'm sure she is motivated, strong and ready to a few risks, all while performing at her very best.

Enjoying our live race coverage?

Subscribe to Cyclingnews for an all-access pass to our unrivalled reporting of WorldTour racing, bike tech and exclusive in-depth features. Plus, access to the Cyclingnews app to follow the action on-the-go!

This is the moment Romina Hinojosa (Lotto Intermarché Ladies) started her ride.

She is the last rider on GC after staying with her teammate Dina Boels finish stage 2.

The Belgian team experienced one of their hardest days on the Tour de France Femmes, losing 3 riders. Dina and Romina fought together for 60 kilometres to finish within time limit and they made it.

Sadly she abandoned the day after but can be proud of her fight.

Lotto Intermarché Ladies only have 3 riders left in the Tour but they will race on.

We have highlighted how the TT is vital for the TDFF GC battle. Today's stage will create the first significant time gaps and so shape how riders will have race in the days to come - on the attack or defence.

The podium of the most recent World Championships time trial gives us an simple indication. There Marlen Reusser (Movistar), Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) and Demi Vollering (FDJ) showed they can gain time on their rivals.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot won the 2025 Tour in the mountains. She has worked hard on her time trialing skills and bike position but admits she is riding into the unknown today.

The time trial will be a race of truth for the French rider.

Read Simone Giuliani's special story.

Back to the racing and 30 riders have started, with ten passing the time check at Lacets de Marsannay, with 11.3 km race, so near half distance of the 21km TT.

Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise) is fastest so far, with 15:49.

That is the first benchmark.

Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise) is the French TT champion, so is racing in the iconic red, white and blue colours.

Romina Hinojosa (Lotto Intermarché Ladies) finishes with a time of 31:24. She is soon beaten by Noémie Abgrall (Ma Petite Entreprise) who sets 30:33.

Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise) beats that and goes into the hot seat with a hot time of 28:50.

Here is Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise) in action.

Our photographers are out along the course to get the best shots.

We love these early pics from the vines of the Côte d’Or. This is Elena Cecchini at speed.

Enjoying our live race coverage?

Subscribe to Cyclingnews for an all-access pass to our unrivalled reporting of WorldTour racing, bike tech and exclusive in-depth features. Plus, access to the Cyclingnews app to follow the action on-the-go!

Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché Ladies) has pulled off a surprise.

She was 10 seconds slower than Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise) at the time check but finished fast and set a new fastest time of 28:49.39, that's just 0.96 second faster than Le Mouël.

Dutch journalist and former rider Thijs Zonneveld rode the TT earlier and highlights the impact of the tail wind, especially off the mid-stage rise.

The time checks show the difference in speed on the different parts of the course.

Zonneveld wrote: "Did a lap of the time trial course. What a racetrack. Wind coming diagonally from behind; after the climb, it goes so fast that you need a parachute to brake on the way down."

60 riders have started the TT, with around 80 still to start.

Check out our interactive times to see who is closest to Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché Ladies). For now she is in the hot seat.

The first kilometre in Gevrey-Chambertin is testing in the town centre streets, with cobbles and road gullies.

It will be important to start fast and perhaps take a few risks.

Daniek Hengeveld (Visma) is the Dutch TT champion and she sets the third-fastest time of 28:59. She is only 9 seconds slower than Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché Ladies).

Lotte Claes (Fenix-Premier Tech) sets a new fastest time of 15:44 at the 11.3km time check.

She is one to watch for the finish.

Urška Žigart (AG Insurance - Soudal Team) is underway.

Next off is Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx) she is racing in the green points jersey.

We know she is fast and has speed and power but we are not expecting her to go full gas in the TT.

Wiebes is likely to try to safe energy for a shot at another stage or in the intermediate sprints.

Lotte Claes (Fenix-Premier Tech) sets the new fastest time of 28:25.

She was 24 seconds faster than Sandrine Tas.

Britain's Millie Couzens (Fenix-Premier Tech) is also fast.

She sets 28:38, to take second place for now.

We had a chance to see the fast descent and it is very fast.

Riders are touching 100km/h even as they ride time trial bikes and perhaps in the aero bars.

Let's hope everyone stays safe.

Time trials are are special bike tech days and we created this photo gallery from the opening stages. It's for our Cyclingnews members and so has a special layout.

There are some great bikes and tech innovations in the TDFF peloton.

These are the TT start times.

The 21km individual time trial takes place in the Côte d'Or vineyards, hills. Riders are on the hunt for gold at the finish line in Dijon, the ride expected to take 27 minutes.

The course begins in the centre of the village, with a flat opening 7km. The route is punctuated by a 1.8km climb to Marsannay-la-Côte, which averages 6.9%.

Once across the top, there is still another one kilometre at 4% gradient to cover to reach Corcelles-les-Monts. The final 9km roll downhill for the finish in Dijon, for the finish on Avenue du Général-de-Gaulle.

Lieke Nooijen (Visma) sets a new fast time of 27:36.

She was 50 seconds faster than Lotte Claes and clearly blasted down the descent at high, high speed.

That will be a hard time to beat.

Zoe Bäckstedt (Canyon) is underway. We will be watching her ride carefully.

The British champion won the TT and the GC at the recent Baloise Ladies Tour. She also defended her British national TT title.

Bäckstedt will set the benchmark amongst the TT specialist and the GC riders.

Staying cool is important.

Zoe Bäckstedt (Canyon) is moving fast. She quickly catches her minute-rider Solène Muller (St Michel - Preference Home-Auber93).

On the climb Bäckstedt also caught Paula Patiño (Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskadi). She is flying!

At the 10km intermediate time check, Bäckstedt is the fastest with a time of 15:30. That is the same time as Lieke Nooijen (Visma).

Bäckstedt went deep on the climb but can now dive down the descent to the finish.

Kirsten Faulkner (EF) sets 28:24.

She was third fastest at the time check and third at the finish.

However Zoe Bäckstedt (Canyon) is on the way to the finish.

It's time for the GC battle to begin.

Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx - Protime) starts her time trial.

All her GC rivals will start after her.

This is the TT start times.

Zoe Bäckstedt (Canyon) lost some precious seconds on the descent and proves that the descewnt is a vital part of the race today.

She sets a time of 27:50. She lost 16 seconds to Lieke Nooijen in 10km on the descent.

All the big-name riders are in the start area for a final bike check and moment of peace.

Once the top 20 take the start ramp, the time between riders will be expanded from one minute to two minutes.

The top pair of contenders in the youth classification will be separated by just one rider, second-placed Isabella Holmgren (Lidl-Trek) starting at 17:00 and then best U24 rider Paul Blasi (UAE Team L'IMAD) going off at 17:04.

Reusser will begin her ride at 17:08, followed by defending Tour champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot (Visma-Lease a Bike) leading a process of the top 10.

Vollering goes off at 17:24, then Kim le Court-Pienaar at 17:26 and Haugset in the yellow jersey at 17:28.

Lieke Nooijen (Visma) spoke about her ride. In truth she was fast on the descent, as well as the climb.

"It's so hot here but I kept pushing to the end. The first part is mostly uplll, where you gain most time, I gave it everything to that point."

Dani Ostanek spoke to Puck Pieterse after she took the polka-dot jersey on stage 3. She is about to start her TT and we will discover is she is a GC contender.

In the next 20 minutes all the GC riders will start their rides.

Marlen Reusser Movistar is off and now so is Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma)

It'll be vital to start fast but surely the world champion is the favourite today.

Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx) set 16:08 at the 9.7km time check. Remember that time for the GC battle.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot does not look very aero on her TT bike. She is rocking and has a high head and body.

She has worked on her TT position but she is a climber and seems to lack the power and aero position adaption.

It will be fascinating to see how much time she loses to Reusser today and what does that mean.

In comparison, Marlen Reusser has a great position, with a flat back but while also putting out the power.

Marlen Reusser sets 15:10 at the time check.

That is 20 seconds faster than Lieke Nooijen (Visma).

Reusser will still have to ride fast on the descent and take some risks.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot sets 16:31 at the time check.

That is 1:20 down Marlen Reusser and the 10km fast descent and flat road to the finish is still to come.

Sigrid Haugset (Uno-X Mobility) starts her TT and so all the riders are out on the course.

Kasia Niewiadoma (Canyon) is 50 seconds faster than Pauline Ferrand-Prévot and only 30 seconds down on Marlen Reusser.

Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD) is only 20 seconds slower than Reusser at the time split.

Marlen Reusser (Movistar) stops the clock in 27:30.

She beats Lieke Nooijen (Visma) by just 4 seconds.

She lost some seconds on the descewnt but did enough to surely win the stage.

Now we wait to see how much her GC rivals lose, especially Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, who is losing minutes to Reusser.

We will have a very different GC tonight.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot finishes in a time of 29:43 She will not be happy with that ride and time loss.

She lost 2:13 to Reusser.

What does that mean to the GC battle now?

Demi Vollering is on the climb and sets at the time check 15:33, only 22 slower than Reusser.

That's an interesting ride and Vollering is in the GC battle.

Sigrid Haugset (Uno-X Mobility) is dressed all in yellow.

She's trying to stay aero on the climb but is losing time after her huge ride yesterday. She sets 17:15 and so is 2:05 down on Reusser.

Sadly she will lose the yellow jersey to Reusser.

Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD) finishes in 28:33. That keeps her in the GC battle.

Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-Oatly) sets 28:24.

Demi Vollering dives down the descent to Dijon.

She opts not to always use the aero bars to stay a little safer.

She sprints out of the corners to keep her speed close to 60km/h on the flat roads to the finish.

Vollering is set to be the best of the rest of the GC contenders, behind expected stage winner and new race leader Reusser.

Demi Vollering (FDJ) stops the clock in 27:48.

Marlen Reusser set 27:30 and so that is a great ride by Vollering.

She was very fast on the descent, doing a negative split compared to Reusser.

Vollering slumps to rhe road and can hardly breath. She gave her absolute all.

As Vollering finished, she stopped her computer and banged her chest twice in recognition of her good ride.

Vollering has limited her losses on Resusser and gained close to 2:00 to Pauline Ferrand-Prévot.

Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance-Soudal) sets 29:53, to slip out of the top five on GC.

Here comes Sigrid Haugset (Uno-X Mobility).

She was already 2:00 slower than Reusser with a kilometre to go and sets a final time of 30:36

That's 3:06 slower than Reusser and so she loses yellow.

Look at the time gaps and think about what it means with all the mountain stages still to come.

The TT has created a new GC and created a new handicap race for the Ventoux finish.

From stage 5 we will see a new Tour de France Femmes.

Marlen Reusser savoured her third Tour stage victory and especially pulling on the leader's yellow jersey, even if she is a perfectionist.

"It wasn’t perfect perfect, but it was good," she said.

"I started well, I did a good climb, but I had a little bit of a problem with my bike and the wind."

Reusser increased her gear options for the fast descent.

"During the recon, it felt a bit different, so I had planned it differently. But in the end, I think I did a good time trial," she said.

Reusser described winning the TT and taking yellow as her Project Dijon. It is mission accomplished, as she has the yellow jersey, just like the colour of mustard.

“It’s the first Tour de France that was really my goal of the year," she said.

"We were starting in Switzerland on the Swiss National Day, and on the fourth day a time trial in Dijon. We’ve been talking about it since Christmas, ‘Project Dijon’, for the yellow colour of the mustard, to win the time trial and maybe take yellow.

"It worked out, and I’m really happy."

Matilda Price and Dani Ostanek are in Dijon speaking to riders and teams for news and analysis. They will soon have a full view and multiple stories on what happened in the time trial.

First up is this quick news on Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma) and how she lost 2:13 to Reusser, 1:59 to Demi Vollering and a minute to all her other GC rivals.

The 2026 Tour de France Femmes continues on Wednesday with stage 5 in the hills of Beaujolais. We're expecting great wines and great racing.

The constantly rolling stage is from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais and includes 2900 metres of elevation gain over 140 kilometres of racing.

The climbing starts immediately with the 9.6km climb of Côte de Cenves, followed by five more classified climbs packed into the opening 75km of the stage.

The final 30km includes Col de Gerbet (4.6 km at 6.5%), it is a climb of two parts, 1.3km of climbing is followed by a flat section before the road pitches up once again for the final 1.4 kilometres, maxing out at 16%.

The bonus second point comes at the bottom of the final climb of the day, Mont Brouilly (3 km at 7.7%), where the final selection will be made. It is just 10 km from the finish line.

Check out full stage preview.

Thanks for joining us for full live coverage of the time trial.

We'll be back on Wednesday with full live coverage of stage 5.

We can't wait. Follow the Femmes!

items.title: Canyon-SRAM announce European bank Scalable Capital as new team backer
items.content:
Canyon-SRAM have confirmed that Scalable Capital, a European bank founded in 2014, have joined the team as a new sponsor.

The logo has been visible on the sides of riders' helmets and on team vehicles taking part in the ongoing Tour de France Femmes.

In a team press release, Scalable Capital is described as "one of Europe’s leading digital banks and investment platforms." It has around 800 employees.

“Having Scalable Capital join Canyon-SRAM is a strong statement for women’s cycling", the team's commercial director Jonas Moslein said in the same statement.

"Beyond the commercial opportunity, we share a common ambition to break down barriers, empower women and inspire the next generation. We firmly believe this partnership has the potential to create a lasting impact far beyond racing.”

Canyon-SRAM said Scalable Capital will be sponsoring both the WorldTour and its 'Generation squad,' its 10-rider Devo' team.

The team cited 'breaches of contract' as the reason for the sudden, mid-season parting of ways with the Polish cryptocurrency company, without providing further details.

items.title: A very Swiss start to the Tour de France Femmes, but what next for women's cycling in Switzerland?
items.content:
Tuesday marks the first full day in France for this year's Tour de France Femmes, after a very Swiss start marked the race's second-ever foreign Grand Départ in five editions.

In many ways, the part of Switzerland we were in – Lausanne, Aigle and Geneva – doesn't feel particularly different from France, as we're only just over the border, but there was a distinct Swiss flavour to the first three stages.

Aside from the Swiss flags lining the roads, the opening stage took place on Swiss National Day, meaning the arrival of the Tour coincided with a festival of celebrations in Lausanne and fireworks in the evening. We paid for everything in CHF, a currency I only ever associate with UCI fines, we saw the United Nations, we did like the locals do and swam in Lake Geneva. A lot of the experience couldn't have felt more Swiss.

The reception of the race in Switzerland felt perhaps mixed, with lots of fans out in Lausanne and Aigle, cheering loudest for Marlen Reusser, and in Geneva the finish was fairly well attended, but for the start the next day, it felt like no one even knew there was a race on, the women's Tour an afterthought to the city that does, admittedly, have bigger things like world peace to worry about.

Switzerland is a country that has put a lot into supporting women's sports – the nation hosted the women's European Championships in football last summer – and indeed women's cycling, with two WorldTour races here in the Tour de Suisse and Tour de Romandie.

But what is going on beyond that? What state of health is women's cycling in Switzerland in? Why host the Tour de France Femmes? Whilst we were here, I dug into some of those questions, speaking to the Swiss riders in the race and race director Marion Rousse to go a bit deeper into the Tour's Swiss excursion.

Within the peloton, there was perhaps the feeling that the Swiss contingent was not quite as big as it could have been, with only two Swiss riders, Marlen Reusser (Movistar) and Noemi Rüegg (EF Education-Oatly), taking the start at home.

There are six Swiss riders in the WorldTour, and one at ProTeam level, but factors like Elise Chabbey's pregnancy and Petra Stiasny's injury after her Vuelta Femenina stage win meant that there weren't as many home riders on the start line as we may have hoped. Compare and contrast with the Rotterdam Grand Départ, when there were 32 Dutch riders in action in 2024.

However, those riders that were here arguably had enough excitement and passion to make up for their lack of numbers.

The biggest star of the pre-race media day, Reusser couldn't stop smiling the whole day, underlining repeatedly how special it was not just to be racing the Tour in Switzerland, but doing it in an edition where she was going for the overall win for the first time.

"I really saw this coming since a long time, and actually my goal was to win the Swiss Championships and stand here with a nice cross. Things didn't go as I wanted, but still, it's super nice," she beamed.

"I've already spent two days in Lausanne, and it feels like there's so much excitement already. Everyone's talking about us, you see bikes everywhere, people have knitted bikes, cycling is alive here.

"I have the feeling that Romandie is more excited about cycling than the rest of Switzerland right now, so I hope that this fever can spread to the rest of Switzerland."

For Reusser's compatriot Noemi Rüegg, it was a race against time to get to the start in Switzerland. She fractured her humerus in a crash at the Vuelta Femenina in May, and the end of the expected 12-week recovery coincided exactly with the start of the Tour de France Femmes in Lausanne.

"It's super special to have the start of the tour here in Switzerland," Rüegg said. "It's been marked in my calendar for a while now. We have really big ambitions, but I think I just want to enjoy it as well, to have family and friends alongside the road, and yeah, enjoy the Swiss crowds."

Racing at home is hardly a novelty for Swiss riders, given they have the Tour de Romandie and Tour de Suisse every year, plus the World Championships in Zurich were less than two years ago, but the Tour de France Femmes, and all the fanfare and international attention that comes with it, is clearly on another level.

When the Tour de France Femmes announced that its first foreign Grand Départ would be in the Netherlands, it felt like the obvious choice, given that perhaps no other nation has contributed so many great stars to the women's peloton.

Whilst Switzerland doesn't have quite the rich women's cycling history of the Netherlands, it also made perfect sense as the place to hold the next Grand Départ on foreign soil. Its proximity to the French border and the Alps makes for straightforward logistics and no air transfers, it's a common stop on the men's WorldTour, and of course Aigle is the home of the UCI, who have been working to build the profile of women's cycling for the past decade.

Marion Rousse explained a bit more about the decision to come to Switzerland when she spoke to the press pre-race.

"For me, starting in Switzerland is a wonderful story," she said. "A foreign start means a lot to us. It shows that, as the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, there is a desire in other countries to share the Tour's prestige, which is what makes it the greatest race in the world and creates that special magic.

"A nice detail in this Swiss connection is that back in 2022, when Wout van Aert won at the top of the Côte de Saint-François, where we’ll be [on stage 1], the first edition of the women's Tour de France was just days away. Switzerland had already put itself forward to host the women's Grand Départ, without even knowing if it would work out. It really demonstrated their commitment to supporting women's sports. That really appealed to us.

"Plus, the route connects Lausanne, the Olympic capital, with Aigle, the home of the UCI, and Geneva, the capital of diplomacy. It’s a really coherent story that I feel reflects the values ​​of our sport perfectly. And going from the Swiss Riviera to the French Riviera [in Nice], it all came together beautifully."

The second stage, starting from Aigle, saw female riders from the World Cycling Centre and the IOC Refugee Olympic Team welcomed to the race for a ceremonial ride before the race, a special moment celebrating the inclusivity and growth of the women's sport, and another special aspect of starting here in Switzerland.

Women's cycling beyond the WorldTour

With two WorldTour races in Switzerland and now the Grand Départ, it would be easy to assume that women's cycling in Switzerland is in rude health, but the story beyond the WorldTour is a little bit more complicated.

It is true that the nation boasts some incredibly strong riders, both on the men's and women's side, and when it comes to World Championships and international events, the top riders do get good support from the Swiss federation. At the World Championships in Rwanda, they fielded five women in the elite road events, two in the U23 races, and two in the junior road race, coming away with a rainbow jersey for Reusser in the TT and third in the junior road race for Anja Grossman.

But if you look a little further down the pyramid, things maybe don't look as well-supported. Since the demise of the Roland Le Dévoluy team, there are no Swiss-registered WorldTour or ProTeams – Swiss men's outfits Pinarello-36.5 and Tudor both support female athletes off-road, but not in the road peloton – and there are just two Continental teams based in Switzerland, the UCI's World Cycling Centre team (WCC) and Nexetis.

As of 2026, there are no lower-level UCI races in Switzerland for women, only the two WorldTour races, which are officially not open to Continental teams or clubs, and the National Championships.

"I think it's getting more and more popular. I think we've, yeah, made really big steps the past few years, thanks to the women's Tour de Suisse and the Tour de Romandie, and now also with this with these two stages here, I think we can hopefully inspire a lot of young girls and boys to start cycling as well," Rüegg said about the state of women's cycling in Switzerland.

"I think we still have a long way to go. If you see that also now we are only two Swiss women in the peloton [at the Tour], so I think we can improve that definitely. But we are already on a really good way compared to a few years ago."

The WCC team is ostensibly there to create a pathway for riders from around the world, mainly outside of western Europe and nations that have little to no professional cycling scene, but several Swiss riders have also turned to the team to get their start in cycling, including Reusser.

Rüegg, meanwhile, found her way through the Akros-Renfer development club, which also kickstarted the careers of Mauro Schmid, Stefan Bissegger and Yannis Voisard, but no longer exists

The next generation seem to only have a few pathways into the WorldTour. Going via mountain biking is one avenue, as mountain biking is arguably even more popular than road racing in Switzerland, and that's worked for riders like Steffi Häberlin.

Many talented riders are also coming up through the Nexetis squad. They have the super-talented Jasmin Liechti (who also started her career with WCC before joining Nexetis in 2025) signing for Canyon-SRAM for 2027, and Ginia Caluori is on her way to Movistar. They do a great job of finding Swiss talent and showing them to the European peloton, but they are only a small outfit, and the funding only goes so far.

"I think there is still some work to do in the younger categories, like under-23 and juniors, because it's pretty hard to find a team that you can race international races with in that age," Rüegg said. "I think Nexetis do an amazing job with that team to help young riders making that step, but I think it's also financially a big challenge to have such a team running and to build on it."

Of course, the impact of an event like the Tour de France Femmes coming to Switzerland, or the expansion of the Tour de Suisse, is hard to quantify in the immediate term. The same is true for the impact and legacy of the football Euros in Switzerland – the women's national team is actually lower in the FIFA rankings right now than before the tournament, but the real impact will likely be some years down the line.

In the short-term, though, Switzerland can count themselves as a growing force in women's cycling. The contingent may be small in this year's Tour, but both riders here are more than capable of winning a stage, one is a World Champion, and though there is work to be done on development pathways, there will be at least two new talented Swiss riders in the WorldTour peloton next year. And if the Tour in Switzerland has inspired young women in the way the riders hope, there should be more on the way.

items.title: 'A tool in this fight' – UCI president David Lappartient backs night-time anti-doping testing in men's Tour de France
items.content:
UCI President David Lappartient has defended night-time anti-doping tests during the men's Tour de France, saying that it was "a tool in this fight" against banned drugs, albeit one that should only be used occasionally.

Both of the most recent winners of the Tour de France, reigning champion Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard, who took the title in 2022 and 2023, were amongst those who had night-time testing during the 2026 race: Vingegaard – who later crashed out on the same day as his test, injured – at 2am and Pogačar at 5am.

Reports later emerged that five other teams had also been tested at some point during the race before 5am, which is not typical under UCI and WADA rules, which restrict normal testing to a 6am to 11pm window.

Being selected for a test, including out-of-hours, is a standard part of anti-doping controls and does not imply any suspicion of, or wrongdoing by, the riders concerned. Neither Pogačar nor Vingegaard have been accused of any anti-doping violation.

Speaking during the ongoing Tour de France Femmes, Lappartient indicated in an interview with and that there would "always be suspicion in cycling." He explained that although he was not in favour of testing overnight on a regular basis, he believed it was a weapon that could help the battle against micro-dosing of illegal substances.

He also said that the absence to date of press releases from the International Testing Agency indicated that there had been no positive tests in the Tour.

"The ITA never make a press release about negative results, only about positive results," said Lappartient.

"We didn’t see any press release in the Tour de France, so it seems there was nothing in the Tour."

The emergence of the night-time testing in the third week of the Tour revived concerns and debate about the current state of the sport's ongoing anti-doping battle.

Whilst not supporting regular night-time testing, Lappartient said the UCI supported the ITA's use of specific tests during that period "because we know that, with micro-dosing EPO, that’s something you can’t detect six or seven hours after. So, for the riders to know that the ITA may come, that’s always a fear."

"We always have suspicion in cycling, due to our past. I know what has been done to fight against doping," he said

"Night testing is a tool in this fight, but it is not a tool to use every day. You must use it very exceptionally. It’s not suspicion about any rider, but it’s a global message to the bunch."

Lappartient's comments back up a press release by the UCI during the third week of the Tour, in which they defended the overnight testing against criticisms made of it by some riders.

"Following a number of reactions in recent days to unannounced anti-doping controls carried out by the International Testing Agency (ITA) during the Tour de France – in particular following the statement issued by the association of professional riders (CPA) – the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) wishes to respond and to reaffirm that the fight against doping is an absolute priority," the statement read.

items.title: Tour de France Femmes Tech Gallery: Lightweight parts, custom paint and a host of clever tech tricks
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
With the men's Tour de France (and with it, the Tadej Pogačar procession) out of the way, now it's time for the real bike race of the summer, the Tour de France Femmes.

Lorena Wiebes might be storming the early stages, but Demi Vollering and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot are gearing up for a mega duel in the GC, while Kim Le Court, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, Marlen Reusser, and Elisa Longo Borghini are all vying to upset the applecart, which has already been somewhat upset already by a barnstorming ride from Norwegian national champion Sigrid Haugset.

As ever, is on the ground covering the racing in all the exciting detail, and here we're going to focus on the tech. In this gallery we've got the usual cohort of nerdy tricks and tidbits, as well as a host of stunning custom paint schemes, and even an appearance from SpongeBob SquarePants (of course!) - you'll have to read on to see what that's all about.

We're going to start at Lidl-Trek, whose bikes are painted in this special design to commemorate Trek's 50th birthday.

Each square marks a specific event in Trek's history.

That's not Santa, it's Trek co-founder Dick Burke.

Describing the smiling banana graphic, Trek says "In 2004, we stubbed out the smoking cafeteria and launched a wellness programme that treated employee health like it mattered – because it does."

There's a page on Trek's website detailing the meaning of - and story behind - each square.

The Lidl-Trek riders were also aboard new Bontrager Aeolus wheels, although we don't know much about them yet.

They also used this neat 3D-printed out-front computer mount, which fits smoothly - and thus aerodynamically - onto the bottom of their head units.

Moving on from Lidl-Trek to Cofidis, this is a pretty cool thing to have on your top tube.

It belongs to Danish national champ Amelie Dideriksen, who's aboard the new Look 795 Blade RS.

The Cofidis team use Campagnolo's Super Record groupset, a rare find given the current Shimano and SRAM duopoly.

The rest of the Look bikes had a fun paint scheme too.

But with Dideriksen's, instead of black paint, it was just clearcoat over the raw carbon, meaning you could see the complex layup of the carbon fibre sheets.

Unsurprisingly, given. the Look bikes, they were aboard Look pedals too.

"It all starts with dreaming." - can you guess whose bike this is?

It's Demi Vollering's, whose S-Works Tarmac SL9 is painted to reflect her status as European road race champion.

This top tube sticker may be a nod to her enjoyment of yoga, a reminder to relax, or perhaps both.

Meanwhile, her former team's bikes - also the Specialized S-Works Tarmac SL9 - have a really cool mismatch custom design to mimic their jerseys.

Close up, the colours and graphics really pop.

They're equipped with SRAM Red groupsets, but everything else is supplied by Specialized and its component subsidiary Roval.

Putting some tape or a gel wrapper inside your out-front computer mount is a simple way to keep it secure and prevent it rattling.

It's been a fruitful start of the race for the Dutch team. Lorena Wiebes has won the first two stages and was in yellow at the time of shooting. To celebrate, the team had adorned her bike with some yellow touches.

Moving on to Visma-Lease a Bike, and this is the Cervelo S5 of Dutch road race champion, Lieke Nooijen.

It bears the same design as the standard bike, but in a colour-switch to reflect the Netherlands flag.

Also, while we're here, that number 274 sticker is the last three digits of the power meter's ANT+ ID, making it easy to pair with your head unit when surrounded by a dozen other team bikes. Simple, but clever.

Here's the usual team bike, with the same design but in the traditional black and yellow colours.

It belongs to team leader, and one of the race favourites, Pauline Ferrand-Prevot. The '2' is a nod to the number of Tour de France stages she's won to date.

This was a nice find on Ferrand-Prevot's bike. To keep the weight down, she's running thru-axles from Chinese brand Overfast.

This was cool too - The custom mount is designed specifically for Visma-Lease a Bike, but the white pen ensures the mechanics can tell if the bolts have loosened, just by looking at it.

The paint job on UAE Team L'IMAD's bikes was nothing special, so the Enve wheels brought some fun to the party instead.

They had this pink geometric finish to the Enve stickers. Curiously, on Blasi Cairol's bike, they also had 'Factory Second' written on the rim, suggesting these weren't up to Enve's preferred standard.

It's unclear what the sticker with UAE Team L'IMAD 26.112 on it means.

Next up, this pink and white design really stood out on Laboral Kutxa's X-Lab AD9 aero bikes, complete with FSA chainset and Power2Max power meter.

The fork legs have a patterned design ot dissimilar to the Trek bikes above.

The fork tips have this massive aero 'blade' protruding from the rear to help smooth airflow as it passes by the fork leg. The red heart is a nice touch too.

While most teams in the WorldTour use bottle cages from Tacx or Elite, Laboral-Kutxa uses cages from lesser known Race One.

We couldn't talk about fun paint jobs without bringing this one up though - Factor One's bikes were painted with this crazy SpongeBob SquarePants theme.

Every element of the bike has been given the SpongeBob treatment.

Even the Wahoo computers were incorporated into the design.

This bike belonged to Human Powered Health's Italian rider, Barbara Malcotti, but they were also painted for Factor's other sponsored team, Ma Petite Entreprise.

Despite riding a Factor bike, Malcotti was using a Specialized saddle. It's rare for women's teams to have a saddle sponsor, since saddle fit is so rider dependent, most are free to choose their own.

The bikes were designed by XXRay, part of the Mighty Jaxx studio.

This is the Ma Petite Enterprise version of the design.

Lotto-Intermarche Ladies' team had the new Orbea Orca Aero at their disposal, mostly in this silver and red finish.

Except Sandrine Tas had this prototype version from before its launch.

The raw carbon was painted with these fluorescent lines to show off specific design elements of the frame.

This one highlights the angular seat stay junction as it meets the seat tube.

It appears that this was the 22nd version of this model ever made.

I really like how the raw carbon can be seen here at the dropouts, showing the different types of carbon fibre used in different parts of the frame.

The lines also highlight the angular design of how the fork leg meets the head tube and down tube. There's also a cut-off section of an inner tube wrapped around the fork leg, which will later be used to shroud the race transponder and make it more aero.

The paint on this Fenix-Premier Tech bike is un assuming at first, but the golden flakes really help it to pop in the sunlight.

Also on the Fenix-Premier Tech bikes, we spotted the newly launched Shimano Dura-Ace wheels, with the part number WF-R9370, confirming they're from a new series of Dura-Ace groupset.

I also liked this little hack nearby, using a zip tie to keep the cable from snagging against the nearby moving parts in the event of a crash.

Despite the men's team – specifically Jasper Philipsen – using prototype pedals at Paris-Roubaix this year, the Fenix-Premier Tech team are still on the R9100 pedals, which carried over when Shimano launched the R9200 series groupset in 2021.

However, we did spot the new pedals elsewhere…

We found them on Eleonora Ciabocco's bike, over at Picnic PostNL.

Details are sparse, but rumours suggest a lower stack height.

They still resemble the existing Shimano Dura-Ace pedals, but in a slightly more refined design.

The big difference, which we learned when Van der Poel and Philipsen failed to swap bikes in Roubaix, is that the two use slightly different pedal-cleat interfaces.

Without knowing these are new, it would be hard to distinguish between these and the older pedals.

At first, this looks totally normal, but on closer inspection, you can see that the E and Y have been filled in using white pen. Presumably worn away by heel rub or damage in transit.

It was found on Katrine Aalerud's Ridley Noah Fast 3.0

These wheels were recently included in Cyclingnews' latest round of wind tunnel testing, albeit the Aero 111 tyre no doubt helps their performance a little.

I can only assume Uno-X have borrowed the power meter ID trick from Visma mentioned above.

I've not seen the DT-Swiss ARC 1100 DiCut wheels laced up using silver hubs before, they look great, and presumably save a bit of weight by having no surface coating.

items.title: 'If there are points up for grabs, then I’m not going to let them slip by' – Puck Pieterse remains focussed on original Tour de France Femmes goal despite taking polka dot jersey
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Dutch rider Puck Pieterse, Fenix-Premier Tech's leader at this year's Tour de France Femmes, is riding high in the general classification heading into today's Dijon time trial.

The 24-year-old, who finished 11th with a stage win on her debut two years ago, currently lies in ninth place, neatly nestled among the big favourites for the yellow jersey, even if stage 3 winner Sigrid Haugset lies two minutes clear of them all.

But Pieterse said before the Grand Départ in Switzerland that she wouldn't be riding for the GC this week. She refused to waver from that plan on Monday evening, having picked up the polka dot jersey during the stage.

"Actually it's still the case, and the polka dot I don't know yet for sure what the plan is," Pieterse told and after finishing among the main group of 37 riders, 2:48 behind Haugset in Poligny.

Earlier in the day, she jumped clear of the peloton twice to lead the race over the first-category Col de la Faucille and Côte de Lajoux, winning 13 queen of the mountain points in the process.

Later in the stage, once Haugset had already launched her 89km solo ride to glory, she added another three to her total, in second place over the Col de la Savine.

All in all, that added up to 18 points for Pieterse, which saw her move clear of Océane Mahé (Ma Petite Enterprise), who started the day in the lead, to don the polka dot jersey on the podium. Mahé has slipped down the standing to fourth after stage 3, and Pieterse now leads Nikola Nosková by four points ahead of stage 4.

Pieterse explained that going for mountain points wasn't a pre-planned strategy. Instead, it was a case of 'well, why not?'

"There was nothing else going on, so if there are points up for grabs, then I’m not going to let them slip by, no," she said before re-asserting that a stage win, to add to her triumph in Liège on stage 4 of the 2024 edition, is her main goal this August.

"I'd quite like to win a stage. So, if that comes at the expense of the polka dots, then so be it. But we’re taking it day by day, and it also depends on how fresh I am," she said.

"I feel good on the bike, so I hope to be able to show myself in the hills… It's a big difference from how I rode in the Tour last year, I think. I think I can definitely stay confident."

items.title: UCI Gravel World Series: Oceania champion Nicole Frain and Jonas Lindberg celebrate solo wins at Hlinsko gravel
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
Nicole Frain (Factor Racing) returned to the top step of the UCI Gravel World Series at Gravel Tour Hlinsko, claiming her fourth series win of the season as she crossed the line solo in the women's elite race. In the men's competition, it was another repeat victor with 3Rides winner Jonas Lindberg (Willing Able Racing) also claiming victory in Czechia.

Lindberg crossed the line of the 131km race with a gap of +2:06 to Joel Suter (Tudor Pro Cycling) while home nation racer Petr Vakoč (Factor Racing) snared the final spot on the podium at the first UCI Gravel World Series race ever held in Czechia.

"The course was perfectly organised and proved to be more demanding than I originally thought," said Vakoč in a post on social media. "Just up and down all day, some smooth gravel, some rougher parts and forest roads and barely any asphalt.

"Left there absolutely everything, together with Joel Suter rode away from big chase group with 40km to go to chase back super strong [Jonas Lindberg] ahead who attacked just after the halfway point of the race. We managed to bring the gap down to thirty seconds inside the last 20km but could not get any closer."

Frain took the women's win at the race in Hlinsko, set on the edge of the Pardubice region, with a gap of 3:28 to Kristýna Zemanová (VIF Cycling) while current series leader, Wendy Oosterwoud (PAS Racing), was third at 6:23 back.

The event in Hlinsko was one of three UCI Gravel World Series races run across the weekend, with Around the Pot in South Africa won by Lisa Bone and Matt Beers while Simon Pellaud and Natalia Franco claimed victory at the high-elevation Bogotá Gravel.

items.title: 'So far, everything is going according to plan' – Pauline Ferrand-Prévot on track after first three Tour de France Femmes stages but now it's time to head into the great unknown
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
So far, so good may be the most apt way of summing up Pauline Ferrand-Prévot's Tour de France Femmes to this point, given the Visma-Lease a Bike rider, who is now far from the unknown quantity she was on her return last year, is looking well set for a spirited title defence in the mountains. But first there is a looming test in the one area where an element of mystery remains – the individual time trial.

The path to the 21km test against the clock on stage 4 has been relatively smooth, even after an unexpectedly explosive start that carried into Monday as the race moved from Switzerland to France. There may have been a key GC day ahead, but there was no sitting quietly to conserve ahead of the time trial battle.

"Of course we knew it was going to be a tough stage, but I didn’t expect it to explode like this," said Ferrand-Prévot's teammate Femke de Vries, who was active in pursuit of the moves. "With the time trial tomorrow, I thought most riders wouldn’t take too many risks today. But the race really came alive on the final climb, and from that moment onwards it was all hands on deck."

As Sigrid Haugset (Uno-X Mobility) rode toward a solo victory, with Lotte Kopecky (SD Worx-Protime) in pursuit, the action among the riders aiming for a high finish overall unfolded on the last climb of the day, even though it was a short category 4 effort that came at 25km from the finish line.

Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance-Soudal) immediately attacked as the road kicked up, with Ferrand-Prévot among those quickly on her wheel. Then Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) delivered a fierce acceleration which momentarily appeared to put the defending champion into difficulty. However, she quickly made her way back into the group of favourites which had split away. Still, the select group ultimately swelled before the line, joined by another bunch of riders which included Ferrand-Prévot's teammate, Marianne Vos, who took third.

Ferrand-Prévot finished tenth on stage 3 while rolling over the line among that first group, which means that after three stages she remains well-placed overall. The French rider is in the main group of favourites, which sits 2:10 behind the stage 3 break winner Haugset, six seconds behind Le Court-Pienaar and four seconds behind Vollering, who grabbed an advantage by taking the time bonus for third on stage 1.

However, the big question now is what the gaps will look like after the 21-kilometre individual time trial on stage 4. Based on recent results, the advantage among the overall contenders on Tuesday naturally falls to the riders who were on the podium of the most recent World Championships time trial, Marlen Reusser (Movistar), Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) and Vollering.

However, just how Ferrand-Prévot may fare when lining up against these riders is one of the great unknowns of this year's Tour. While the Visma-Lease a Bike rider once may have been the French national time trial champion and lined up in a race against the clock with some of her current rivals – like Van der Breggen and Niewiadoma – that was more than a decade ago.

Since her return to the road at the start of last season, Ferrand-Prévot has only delivered one time trial in competition, and that doesn't really deliver any indication of her individual prowess given it was in a team effort at the Vuelta Femenina last year, where the squad came in at the middle of the field.

Still, there is no doubting that Ferrand-Prévot is among that small group of competitors who seem to be able to consistently rise to the occasion through focused training, and there is no doubt that the rider has done plenty of that since it was announced late last year that there would be a time trial in the route of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes.

"I really like this kind of challenge, so I took it very seriously, and I think I did my homework quite well," Ferrand-Prévot, who made time trial efforts a regular part of her routine and tested herself on simulations of the stage 4 effort, said in a pre-race media conference.

The rider – who has an Olympic gold medal in mountain biking and also in 2015 simultaneously held the world cyclocross, mountain bike and road titles – is nothing if not adaptable when new cycling challenges are presented. Still, the lack of recent time trial competition presents an unknown.

"So far, everything is going according to plan," said sports director Jos van Emden in a team media release. "Pauline is in a good position, and tomorrow we will aim for the best possible result in the time trial.

"We are not focused on the others, but purely on ourselves. The goal is to ride as hard and as well as possible. In the end, we will see what the result is."

items.title: Extra clothing checks at Tour de France Femmes after reports riders may be padding bras for aero gains
items.content:
Riders at the Tour de France Femmes can expect more detailed clothing checks before stage 4's time trial after reports that riders may be using additional padding in their bras to gain an aero advantage after the UCI issued a special warning about items "which could modify riders’ morphology".

published a story on Sunday about this potential issue, noting that riders have sometimes appeared to have a larger chest size during time trials compared to road races, and reporting that several WorldTour teams have voiced their concerns over riders' artificially changing their breast size using padding during races.

An increased volume in the chest area can have significant aerodynamic gains, as it redirects the airflow around the body, for both men and women.

Chest fairings, which are essentially items put down the front of the jersey to change the shape of the chest, have been found to be effective in saving watts and therefore time, particularly in aero positions for cyclists and triathletes, and have been banned by several governing bodies, including in cycling.

Lidl-Trek's head of technical and innovation told that his team have tested different kinds of bras and found some more padded bras to have benefits, but did say that it's not something the team have actually used in racing.

Under articles 1.3.032 and 1.3.033 of the UCI rules, riders may not use any objects to artificially change their morphology, and any kind of fairings or textured fabrics are banned.

At the 2025 World Championships in Rwanda, riders from Belgium had their radio pockets on their chest rather than their back, with no penalties, and riders have sometimes ridden with bottles down the front of their jersey, though the UCI has tried to police that.

For male riders, the policing of chest fairing use is relatively easy, but it becomes complicated for women, who all have different sized breasts and use all different kinds of sports bras during races.

Some riders have opted to race without a sports bra – that often minimises and compresses the breasts – for aero gains, but reports that some riders are doing the opposite, using padding in their bras to increase their breast size or alter their chest shape in a way that is difficult to police or detect.

However, since story caused a stir in the paddock, the UCI jury did something unusual on Monday evening and added an extra warning to the Tour de France Femmes communiqué ahead of the stage 4 time trial.

"Riders must be to the final checks before the race (bikes and outfit) no later than 10 minutes before their respective start time," the communique reads, which is normal, but then it goes on to say: "Particular attention will be paid to compliance with article 1.3.032 of the UCI regulations, including nonessential elements and clothing or other items/accessories worn by a rider (including but not limited to helmets, glasses, shoes or in-race communication devices) which could modify riders’ morphology."

It's not often a warning like this is specifically given before a time trial.

The question, though, is how will these checks take place without being invasive? According to some teams have suggested that riders could be checked in a private tent by a female jury member to ensure there is no padding or extra material in their sports bra or clothing, but even this likely feels invasive to some.

What's more, the rule is a likely grey area, with no defined amount of padding or support a bra may or may not have, with different women having different needs and preferences.

However, with the UCI sharing the special warning on Monday, it suggests that they will be attempting to carry out extra checks on Tuesday.

items.title: Tour de France Femmes stage 4 time trial start times – Bäckstedt, Reusser, Vollering among second half of starters taking on 21km ITT
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
After a hilly day on the third day of the Tour de France Femmes saw a surprise breakaway rider take the yellow jersey, stage 4 is set to be even more unpredictable with a 21km individual time trial.

After the absence of a race against the clock last year, the ITT returns and this time has a midpoint ascent of nearly 2km to disrupt the rhythm of time trial specialists and leave the door open for climbers.

"You really can't predict what it's going to be like, whether it's going to be a super good day for the climbers or if it's going to be a super good day for the time trial riders,” Zoe Bäckstedt (Canyon-SRAM), the reigning U23 ITT World Champion told ahead of stage 3.

The 21km individual time trial takes place in the Côte d'Or department, filled with an abundance of vineyards, hills and historic cities. Riders are on the hunt for gold at the finish line in Dijon, the ride expected to take 27 minutes.

Riders begin with a relatively flat opening 7km. The route is punctuated by a 1.8km climb to Marsannay-la-Côte, which averages 6.9%. Once across the top, there is still another one kilometre at 4% gradient to cover to reach Corcelles-les-Monts. The final 9km roll downhill for the finish in Dijon, for the finish on Avenue du Général-de-Gaulle.

The last ITT at the Tour was a 6.3km flat shootout in Rotterdam, won by Demi Vollering. There's no comparison on the route, but there are similar adversaries looking to put time into each other as before.

Stage 3 winner Sigrid Haugset (Uno-X Mobility), wearing the yellow jersey as the last rider down the start ramp in Gevrey-Chambertin on Tuesday, has just over two minutes on many of the favourites, including ITT elite world champion Marlen Reusser (Movistar). What will be interesting to watch will be Haugset's time, as she finished 11th in the ITT at last year's World Championships, going 3:15 slower than Reusser. Haugset has 2:06 on Vollering, who had a crash on stage 3 and will be evaluated prior to Tuesday's start, and the buffer to Bäckstedt is a hefty 6:22.

The first rider of 138 will be Mexican rider Romina Hinojosa (Lotto-Intermarché), the clock starting at 14:51 CEST. From the second half of the start list, Pan American ITT winner Kristen Faulkner (EF Education-Oatly) will take her turn at 16:20. Nine riders and nine minutes later, Bäckstedt will then take her turn.

Once the top 20 take the start ramp, the time between riders will be expanded from one minute to two minutes. The top pair of contenders in the youth classification will be separated by just one rider, second-placed Isabella Holmgren (Lidl-Trek) starting at 17:00 and then best U24 rider Paul Blasi (UAE Team L'IMAD) going off at 17:04.

Reusser will begin her ride at 17:08, followed by defending Tour champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot (Visma-Lease a Bike) leading a process of the top 10. Vollering goes off at 17:24, then Kim le Court-Pienaar at 17:26 and Haugset in the yellow jersey at 17:28.

items.title: 'The goal is to minimise the loss' – Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney fully realistic about Tour de France Femmes time trial abilities
items.content:
When an individual time trial was announced as part of the Tour de France Femmes route last autumn, some riders would have been rubbing their hands together with glee and others would have felt a wave of disappointment. Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) was definitely in the latter category.

Despite being a Grand Tour winner, the race against the clock has never quite been Niewiadoma-Phinney's favoured discipline. Whilst she can match all of her big rivals in the climbs, she can't harness the power on the TT bike in the same way.

Ahead of the stage 4 effort to Dijon on Tuesday, Niewiadoma-Phinney was making no excuses or exaggerations about her hopes for the 21km effort.

"It's not a secret that I'm not a TT specialist, so personally for me the goal is to minimise the loss as much as possible," she told on Monday.

"I know I'm not going to be shining there, so basically the goal is to have as little time lost as possible."

With the 2km Lacets de Marsannay climb in the middle of the TT, it is in theory slightly more weighted towards the climbers than the pure power TT specialists, but it's what comes after the winding climb that makes the stage particularly tricky.

"Normally I would say yes [you could gain time on the climb], but with the characteristic of this particular course, you have a downhill that requires you to still be on the pedals, it's not that you're just getting in position and cruising. You still need to have something left for the finish line and for the entire downhill, you don't want to lose much time there," Niewiadoma-Phinney explained.

"I have no idea, I'm not a TT specialist. In some ways it sucks, but in some ways also it's exciting to see what I can do."

Just because it's not her favourite discipline doesn't mean Niewiadoma-Phinney hasn't been putting the effort in to improve her TT, though, saying as early as the last World Championships that that was a key goal for her over the next couple of years. So there was no sense that she was overly worried about stage 4.

"Definitely I spent a fair amount of time on a TT bike. I know I have power, I also know I did not really have the right position, or I was not able to hold the position, so I think now I just need to stay calm and be fast," she said.

And though she knows that even her best effort may still see her lose time on many rivals, the TT isn't where this race will be won, and there are still chances for a rider like her in the five stages after the TT.

"I think so," she said when asked if she could take back any time lost. "Maybe not on Demi [Vollering], because of course she's super strong, but with riders like Marlen [Reusser], I think that maybe we can find opportunities to gain time on her."

As for the race in general, Niewiadoma-Phinney has so far avoided any drama, sitting comfortably in eighth on the same time as all the main GC contenders.

"So far, so good," she said of the opening weekend.

"It's not been a real smash happening for the GC contenders, it was a classic first two stages, quite hectic and nervous in the peloton, but still quite conservative riding for most of us."

items.title: A plan months in the making and 'a very hard worker' – How Uno-X Mobility grabbed double success at the Tour de France Femmes
items.content:
Uno-X Mobility have a huge amount to celebrate at the Tour de France Femmes on Monday evening, with Sigrid Haugset putting in an enormous ride to secure not only the team's first Tour stage win, but pull on the yellow jersey, too. But this win was far from spontaneous.

In fact, Uno-X have had this stage circled for several weeks, and have been down to southeast France with Haugset to recon these roads, so they knew exactly what they wanted to do on stage 3.

Attacking more than 80km from the finish and riding solo for over half the stage may not have been the exact way anyone expected her to win, but that knowledge only boosted Haugset's confidence in the finale, which was essential when she had Lotte Kopecky (SD Worx-Protime) chasing her down.

Once the emotional celebrations at the bus had calmed down, Haugset's DS and performance director gave their insights into the team's biggest win yet.

"We just said to stay focused, keep it cool, eat, drink, focus on a good line, and don't give up," Uno-X DS Nicolas Marche said at the finish, explaining what the team car was telling Haugset as Kopecky came within 10 seconds of her.

"As I say, we knew the course very well, she knew it very well, we came here to recon one or two months ago, so we knew exactly the route so we knew exactly - where it's important to keep energy and to pull. We knew also that Kopecky in this downhill will be faster, also a bit more heavy and stuff. So we kept believing, but it's just incredible.

"We really just encouraged her to keep going, no matter if Kopecky came up, it looked like yellow, so it was a win-win anyway," performance director Jesper Bundgaard Vinkel added. "So we just pushed her all we could."

Though many people may have looked at Kopecky as the strongest rider, her team knew the Norwegian had the strength to win.

"Sigrid is working so hard every day; she's a special girl, she's not been that long in cycling, so I don't imagine many people really know how strong she is," Bundgaard Vinkel said.

"I think we put in a lot of hard work, everybody in the team, Sigrid as well, and she's really a fighter. We picked this stage before the start of the Tour, this one and another one, to go full-in, and she did, and it was incredible that it worked out."

Their faith didn't falter when Kopecky made inroads, as they felt that Haugset was still stronger where it counted.

"Actually, Kopecky and Sigrid we saw on the final climb were a bit the same in terms of physical level, and then we had a very technical downhill where we know that Kopecky [is strong]. [Sigrid] almost crashed actually, and she [Kopecky] took time there. We knew that is a big strength of Kopecky, and we knew the final was actually always slightly up and down and really about the physical level, so we kept pushing," Marche explained.

"At 10 seconds we said 'Now it's you and a TT, and physically you are on the same level as Kopecky so just keep going and keep going to the line and don't give up'. We really believed in it, and she showed it."

Haugset isn't a name that all viewers will be familiar with, but those who have been watching carefully will have taken note of her impressive rides in hard races so far this year, with her results sheet probably not quite reflecting how strong she has been.

"She's just an amazing rider to work with, always happy, always smiling. A very hard worker, I think I never saw a rider working so hard, so dedicated to what she is doing, and I think now she showed to the world who she is," is how Marche described the 27-year-old, who only started racing professionally in 2022.

"I think she showed it already a little bit this year, her first year in WorldTour; she came from Continental, she developed. This year was a development process with her, we took the time, we don't put pressure, and I think in the Giro we saw what she's capable of. She was there to support, and at the end she had some impressive stages, especially the last stage of the Giro; she was with the best, it was all about physically.

"So we know what she's able to do, and that's the goal actually, to come to this Tour with Sigrid to actually take an opportunity like today and taking [the win] already today, the first one that we [highlighted], it's just unbelievable, and I think more to come. The Tour is only just starting."

Indeed, the Tour is only just starting, and so are Uno-X's ambitions. After achieving their goal of moving their men's team up into the WorldTour – and in fact winning a men's Tour stage in 2025 and wearing the yellow jersey this year – the next goal for the Norwegian team is about pushing their women's programme to the next level. Haugset pulling on yellow on Monday, even if she may not expect to hold it for long, is the next big step in that journey.

"We have a big goal in the team to win the yellow jersey in the overall in 2030 with the men and women, so I think this summer shows that we are on the way," Bundgaard Vinkel said.

Marche was similarly proud: "We are in the process of this goal and dream, but I think we are showing who we are now."

items.title: 'We have to do a checkup this evening and see how it goes tomorrow' – Demi Vollering suffers early crash on challenging stage 3 of Tour de France Femmes
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The Dutch rider fell along with new mountains classification leader Puck Pieterse and world champion Magdeleine Vallieres as the peloton raced up the day's opening climb, just 13km into the race.

Vollering avoided serious injury and was quick to get back on her bike. However, after warming down following the stage finish in Poligny, she looked to be walking gingerly after climbing off her time trial bike.

Vollering's team refused media requests for both her and her teammate Célia Gery after the stage, which was run through the Jura hills in temperatures reaching 35°C. Team directeur sportif Nicolas Maire was on hand to break down the stage and said that Vollering will undergo further checkups ahead of Tuesday's stage 4 time trial.

"She looks OK. We'll try to see with the physio how she feels, but we have to do a checkup this evening and see how it goes tomorrow," he told before admitting that he had expected more action from the stage, which saw a group of 37 eventually come together behind phenomenal solo winner Sigrid Haugset and second-placed Lotte Kopecky.

"We were expecting a bit more from the stage, but I think at one point there is like a poker game, and nobody wants to play for the other, so we lost time," he said, remarking on the time gap to Haugset.

The Norwegian launched her astounding attack 89km from the finish line, holding off a charging Kopecky on the road to Poligny. Further back, a larger chase group of GC favourites went clear and then regrouped with those dropped behind as their deficit ballooned to almost three minutes as Vollering and fellow GC contenders Kim Le Court-Pienaar and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney traded blows over the day's final hills.

"I would say it's a pity for all the GC contenders, but I just say that Uno-X played well and they deserve the win and the yellow jersey," he added.

"The Tour is still long, and we'll fight in the next day to come back in the GC, but yeah, we were expecting a bit more from this stage. We tried to be in the breakaway with Célia, but it didn't work exactly as we wanted

"I think we missed the move with Kopecky, and that's a bit of a pity if we just look at our race."

Maire also said that he expected a bit more work at the front of the chase from Visma-Lease a Bike in particular. The Dutch team had reigning champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot and Femke de Vries among the lead group, later joined by their sprinter Marianne Vos on the flatter run-in to Poligny.

"There are a lot of riders like Le Court-Pienaar and Vos who can come here and play for a win, especially without Wiebes. So, I was expecting that they would chase a bit more. Nobody wants to ride for the other, and we arrive at almost three minutes," he said, before turning attention to the time trial, a 21km test against the clock to Dijon.

"I would say I expect a good TT from Demi, but we know that, for example, normally she will lose time on Reusser, on maybe Van der Breggen," he concluded.

"Normally, she can win some seconds on some GC contenders, so that's what we are looking for. If she plays really well, I think she can for sure try to be on the podium on this stage."

items.title: Manchester United supporters groups in uproar over suspension of season tickets
items.author: Exclusive by Jamie Jackson
items.content:
• Fans claim they are being ‘treated as suspects’

  • Club planning to reinstate tickets before season begins

Manchester United’s official Fans’ Forum, Manchester United Suppor­ters Trust (Must), The 1958 and five other such groups have complained to the club over supporters being “treated as suspects” after some had season tickets suspended as part of a move to stop the illegal reselling of seats.

United last week contacted fans who used six or more devices to access accounts linked to the club or to forward tickets, as in their view this suggested the potential buying of seats to resell. Members are allowed only to forward tickets to other members, or sell them back to United.

items.title: Why did Manchester United pay Chelsea £48m for Andrey Santos?
items.author: Ryan Benson
items.content:
Michael Carrick’s first signing is a surprise, but the Brazil midfielder will help the team deal with Casemiro’s exit

Andrey Santos moving from Chelsea to Manchester United was not on our summer transfer window bingo card, but the Brazilian has become Michael Carrick’s first signing. United desperately needed reinforcements in midfield, especially after Casemiro’s departure and Manuel Ugarte’s long-term injury, so deals for Santos and Youri Tielemans will be welcomed by fans.

Tielemans looks like particularly good business – he captains Belgium, has made 244 appearances in the Premier League and was available for £35m – but Santos is a more curious choice. He was often a backup player for Chelsea last season as they finished seven places and 19 points behind United; he is not the finished article, and played for one of United’s rivals. Since Alex Ferguson retired 13 years ago, United had only signed four players from their “big six” rivals: Juan Mata, Nemanja Matic, Mason Mount (all Chelsea) and Alexis Sánchez (Arsenal).

items.author: Jamie Jackson
items.content:
• West Ham winger available for right price after relegation

  • Rashford has two years remaining on United contract

Manchester United will turn their attention towards Crysencio Summerville should Marcus Rashford leave this summer, with the West Ham winger’s potential fee around £30m. Summerville is viewed as having the right profile in regards to a left-sided forward to replace the England international.

Since relegation to the Championship, West Ham are open to selling the 24-year-old Dutchman providing they receive a suitable offer. Summerville, who was part of the Netherlands’ World Cup campaign, has three years remaining on his contract.
